'''Meredith Charles "Flash" Gourdine''' (September 26, 1929 – November 20, 1998) was an American athlete, engineer and physicist. His nickname, "Flash" Gourdine, is a reference to comic strip character [[Flash Gordon]].<ref name=NatAcademyPress>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/memorialtributes0000unse/page/104/mode/2up |title=Memorial tributes. Volume 9 |publisher=Washington, D.C. : National Academy Press |year=2001 |pages=104–106 |chapter=Meredith C. Gourdine 1929-1998 by Allen F. Rhodes}}</ref>

==Early life==
Gourdine graduated from [[Brooklyn Technical High School]]. He earned a BS in [[Engineering physics|Engineering Physics]] from [[Cornell University]] in 1953, where he was selected for membership in the [[Quill and Dagger]] society.<ref name=CulturalNAS>{{Cite web|title=Meredith Gourdine|url=http://www.cpnas.org/aahp/biographies/meredith-gourdine.html|access-date=2020-06-10|publisher=Cultural Programs of the [[National Academy of Sciences]]}}</ref><ref name=TellurideAssociation>{{Cite web|date=2018-02-14|title=Telluride's Olympians: Meredith 'Flash' Gourdine CB50 and Bonnie St. John SP81|url=https://www.tellurideassociation.org/blog/tellurides-olympians-meredith-flash-gourdine-cb50-bonnie-st-john-sp81/|access-date=2020-06-10|website=Telluride Association|language=en-US}}</ref> In 1960, he earned a Ph.D. in Engineering Physics from the [[California Institute of Technology]] on a Guggenheim fellowship.<ref name=NatAcademyPress/>

== Career ==
=== Athletic career ===
At the [[Athletics at the 1952 Summer Olympics|1952 Summer Olympics]] in [[Helsinki]], while he was still an undergraduate student at Cornell, he won a silver medal for the long jump, one and a half inch short of [[Jerome Biffle]]'s gold medal jump.<ref name=TellurideAssociation/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Carwell |first=Hattie |title=Blacks in Science |publisher=Exposition Press |year=1977 |isbn=0-682-48911-5 |edition=First |location=Hicksville, N.Y. |pages=50–51}}</ref>

=== Scientific career ===
[[File:From Dreams to Reality - A Tribute to Minority Inventors.ogg|thumb|Meredith Gourdine is featured in this USPTO film from 1989. Skip to 14:10 for the start of the section on Gourdine, which includes him speaking about his work on airport fog dispersal system, his time as an Olympian, and his work in the late 1980's.]]
During the last three years of his Ph.D. program (1958-1960), Gourdine worked as a senior research scientist at the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]].<ref name=LemelsonMIT>{{Cite web |title=Meredith C. Gourdine|publisher=[[Lemelson Foundation|Lemelson]]-[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT Program]] |url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/meredith-gourdine |access-date=2020-06-10}}</ref> After graduation, he worked for Plasmadyne Corporation and [[Curtis-Wright Corporation]], then in 1964, he founded a research and development firm, Gourdine Laboratories, in [[Livingston, New Jersey]].<ref name=NatAcademyPress/> In 1973 he founded Energy Innovations, a company that produced direct-energy conversion devices in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]]. The companies developed engineering techniques to aid removing smoke from buildings and disperse fog from airport runways, and converting low-grade coal into inexpensive, transportable and high-voltage electrical energy.<ref name=CulturalNAS/>

Gourdine was inducted to the Dayton, Ohio, Engineering and Science Hall of Fame in 1994,<ref name=TellurideAssociation/> was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1991, was a member of the Black Inventors' Hall of Fame, a member of the [[Army Science Board]], and served as a Trustee of Cornell University.<ref name=TellurideAssociation/><ref name=NatAcademyPress/> He was an expert in [[electrogasdynamics]], the generation of electrical energy based on the conversion of the kinetic energy contained in a high-pressure, ionized, moving combustion gas (e.g., [[Ion wind]]).<ref name=CulturalNAS/>  He specialized in devising applications, including electric precipitator systems.  He also invented the Focus Flow [[heat sink|Heat Sink]], used to cool computer chips.<ref name=LemelsonMIT/>

Gourdine was granted a total of over 30 U.S. patents.<ref name=LemelsonMIT/>

He was involved in a number of civic groups during his career, including New York Mayor Lindsay's Task Force on Air Pollution, President Lyndon Johnson's Advisory Panel on Energy, and President [[Richard Nixon]]'s Task Force on Small Business.<ref name=NatAcademyPress/>
